subject: TTFT & streaming SLOs — post-demo next steps
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>

Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya@redwood.ai>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi@redwood.ai>

Subject: TTFT & streaming SLOs — post-demo next steps

Hi Sara — thanks again for the time today, and great to see Avista's demo. Quick recap and proposed next steps on the performance requirements we discussed: 

Summary of requirements we captured on the call:
- Time-to-first-token (TTFT) target: 200–300 ms (95th percentile) for the primary user flow
- Streaming delivery: customer prefers WebSocket; SSE acceptable as fallback
- Chunk cadence: target 50–100 ms between chunks for human-facing streaming UI (aiming for ~80 ms)
- Throughput: baseline 100 requests/sec with bursts to 250 req/sec during peak windows
- Concurrency: expected steady-state concurrency of 20 simultaneous sessions; burst concurrency up to 60 for short periods
- Fallback behavior: must degrade gracefully to a smaller model variant with TTFT < 400 ms if primary path is constrained

Questions / asks for next steps:
1) Can you confirm the 95th percentile TTFT target at 250 ms or indicate if 200 ms is required?
2) Can you share a representative request payload (size + typical prompt) and expected token output length so we can size batching/KV cache?
3) Do you have a preference for WebSocket subprotocols or auth approach (JWT vs. signed headers)?

Attachments: demo-recording.mp4 (call recording), ttft-measurement-spec.pdf (draft of how we can measure TTFT end-to-end)

Next steps I propose:
- If you confirm targets, schedule a 60-min technical deep-dive with our inference engineers to validate pipeline and propose a performance plan (A/B config if needed)
- We'll run a short spike to measure cold-start and warm TTFT on our staging infra using your sample payloads

Proposed availability: Mon/Tue next week (Mar 5–6) afternoon PT.

Thanks — looking forward to aligning.

—

Marissa — thanks for the clear recap. Confirming from Avista side: 
- We can accept TTFT 95th <= 250 ms for the primary flow. 200 ms would be ideal but 250 ms is acceptable as the SLA target.
- WebSocket is our preferred streaming transport (we currently use a lightweight JWT for auth on ws connections)
- Chunk cadence: we aim for ~80 ms between chunks for conversational UI (we can be flexible +/- 30 ms)
- Throughput: baseline 120 req/sec, with short bursts up to 300 req/sec during peak campaigns
- Concurrency: steady-state ~25, bursts up to 75

From: Aditya Rao <aditya@redwood.ai>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 1 Mar 2028 16:20:05 -0700
Subject: RE: TTFT & streaming SLOs — post-demo next steps

Marissa / Rishi — quick internal note on feasibility and things to validate before the deep-dive: 

- TTFT components: auth handshake (WS upgrade), model cold-start, tokenizer overhead, first-token kernel path. For 250 ms 95th we need to ensure warm KV cache for common prefixes and avoid disk-based weights on request path.
- Streaming choice: WebSocket is easier for fine-grained cadence control. We'll want to agree on chunk framing and whether we stream token-by-token or small batches (we recommend batching 4–8 tokens per chunk to reduce syscall overhead while keeping cadence ~60–100 ms).
- Batching and throughput: at 120–300 req/sec, we should plan for dynamic batching (sub-ms scheduling granularity) with size caps to maintain TTFT. Also consider prefix caching for repeated system prompts to reduce effective token work per request.
- Fallback model: propose a 1) large model (primary, quantized), 2) mid model (fast, lower quality) for graceful degradation. Need to validate quality delta and cold-start times.

Action items for the deep-dive prep:
- Marissa: get sample payloads and expected token counts from Sara.
- Rishi / infra: prepare an internal runbook for how we measure TTFT (client-side vs. server-side markers), and a short spike plan for cold-start timings.
- I'll draft a suggested chunking cadence matrix (token_batch_size vs expected chunk latency) and share ahead of the call.

FYI: this one looks like a good candidate for a short A/B between: (A) aggressive batching + larger chunks vs (B) smaller token batches at lower latency but higher cost. We should present cost/latency tradeoffs.

- Aditya
Senior Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference
